Operator: Dear ladies and gentlemen, welcome to the Merck Investor and Analyst Conference Call on second quarter 2026. As a reminder, all participants will be in a listen-only mode. I am now handing over to Florian Schröder, Head of Investor Relations, who will lead you through this conference. Please go ahead, sir.

Florian Schröder (Head of Investor Relations, Merck): Thank you very much, Heidi. Good afternoon, good morning, everyone, and welcome to our Q2 2026 results call. Thank you for joining us today. My name is Florian Schröder, and I'm the Head of Investor Relations at Merck. In our Q2 call today, Kai Beckmann, Group CEO, will begin with sharing an update on first steps since we announced our new strategic direction in May. Kai will provide a brief overview of our business performance and key developments in the second quarter as part of his executive summary.
Helene von Roeder, Group CFO, will guide you through the detailed financial overview. Before we move into the Q&A session, where we will be joined by Jean-Charles Wirth, CEO of Life Science, Danny Bar-Zohar, CEO of Healthcare, and Benjamin Hein, CEO of Electronics, Kai will share our updated outlook and guidance with you. With that, I'm pleased to hand it over to Kai to kick us off.

Kai Beckmann (Chairman of the Executive Board and Group CEO, Merck): Thank you, Florian, and good afternoon, good morning, and thanks to you all for joining us today. Before we get to the numbers, let me first give you a sense of where we stand strategically and highlight the milestones we have achieved in recent months since announcing our strategic direction in May. Each of these milestones addresses the evolving expectations of our customers and patients in an increasingly complex world.
Geopolitical tensions, shifting trade dynamics, active policy debates, and accelerating AI-driven technology rates are all shaping the environment in which we operate. In this context, only a clear plan and disciplined execution will move us closer to the sustainable, profitable growth we are building for our company. Allow me to share a few early proof points. Let me start with the signing of a definitive agreement to acquire Bio-Techne operation on June 25th.
Subject to regulatory approval and closing, Bio-Techne's complementary portfolio of high-quality reagents, analytical instruments, and diagnostic systems for precision medicine is expected to be immediately accretive to sales growth and margins. In parallel, we continue to invest in the capacity required to scale our manufacturing and R&D in Electronics, delivering precise, reliable, and scalable solutions across the semiconductor value chain. In June, we opened a new metrology and inspection site near Grenoble, France.
This EUR 20 million investment will expand our capacity for M&I tools in a key semiconductor hub. Our rare diseases portfolio continues to show strong momentum, and our pipeline has also advanced. Xevinapant and GOMEKLI both delivered quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year growth. In addition, Pimicotinib generated first sales in China and preparations for a U.S. launch are underway. The FDA granted breakthrough therapy designation for enpatoran for the treatment of lupus with active cutaneous manifestations.
The first patient was dosed in a phase III trial evaluating our anti-CEACAM5 antibody-drug conjugate, Precem-TcT for the third-line treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer. I stop here for today. Going forward, we will continue to share further proof points demonstrating that we are focusing investments where we see the strongest growth opportunities. We will make it easier for customers to work with us through more integrated solutions, we will share capabilities more effectively across the company.
We will continue to use partnerships and acquisitions where they accelerate progress. With that, let me turn to our operational and financial performance in the second quarter. Q2 was a pretty robust quarter. Following a solid start into the year, we continued to build growth momentum in the second quarter. Organic sales growth accelerated to 4.1%, supported by strong contributions from Life Science and Electronics.
In Life Science, growth was broad-based across all regions. Process Solutions again delivered strong growth, with sales up 15% organically. As a reminder, we expect the growth profile to normalize in the second half of the year. Advanced Solutions also contributed solid growth, while Discovery Solutions showed slight growth in a still muted market environment. In Healthcare, as I pointed out, rare diseases continued to make a meaningful contribution.
To better align with our operational structures, we have reorganized the remaining franchises. Cardiometabolic is now reported on a standalone basis, while Fertility & Endocrinology has been established as a newly created franchise. Both were broadly stable in the quarter. Specialty Care, which comprises of neurology and oncology assets, drove the overall organic decline in Healthcare, mainly reflecting the impact from Mavenclad in the U.S. and continued competition for Verzenio.
In Electronics, organic growth accelerated significantly to 12% in Q2. Semiconductor Solutions delivered very strong organic growth of 17%, fueled by continued momentum in advanced nodes. Optronics remained broadly stable, while headwinds in consumer electronics end markets are expected to increase further. As a result, we delivered on our ambition to generate profitable organic growth for the group while continuing to invest in innovation. EBITDA pre-margin expanded year-over-year by 1.6 percentage points to 29.4%.
Based on these robust results, we are raising our full year guidance, and I will share the details with you later in this call. Looking now at the group bridge in more detail on page six. Supported net sales increased by 3.4% year-over-year in Q2. Organic sales growth reached 4.1%, driven by Life Science and Electronics. A negative currency impact amounted to -1.1%, portfolio effects contributed 0.4%.
In Q1, organic growth of 2.9% was more than offset by disproportionate foreign exchange headwinds and negative portfolio effects. This quarter, the entire mix of organic growth, FX, and portfolio effects improved visibly, leading to an accelerated growth momentum. Organic EBITDA pre-growth was pleasing 9.3%, also driven by favorable comps in Electronics in Q2 2025. I'm handing over to Helene now to share further details.

Helene von Roeder (Member of the Executive Board and CFO, Merck): Thank you very much, Kai, a warm welcome also from my side. With that, let's dive into the overview of key financials on page eight. Net sales increased from EUR 5.255 billion in Q2 2025 to EUR 5.434 billion in Q2 2026. As mentioned already, this is driven by solid organic growth and easing currency headwinds, while portfolio effects in Healthcare and Electronics largely balanced each other out. EBITDA pre increased from EUR 1.46 billion to EUR 1.6 billion.
The organic increase by 9.3% was driven primarily by Life Science and Electronics, while foreign exchange and portfolio effects were close to neutral, leading to reported growth of 9.4%. EPS pre increased by 6.9% to EUR 2.16, this is achieved despite a visible increase in interest costs related to the financing of SpringWorks acquisition. However, for the full year, we slightly reduce our interest cost guidance, as you can see in the appendix. Operating cash flow increased moderately by 6.7% to EUR 605 million, which does not tell the full story.
Temporary effects are partially offsetting structural improvements, I will come back to this in a minute. Net financial debt increased to EUR 9.2 billion as of June 30th, mainly due to the dividend payment. The increase in working capital is largely a Q1 effect, with smaller increases in Q2, essentially relating to foreign exchange effects. One housekeeping item which I would like to flag already today is the potential impact of the implementation of IFRS 18. IFRS 18 will become effective as of January 2027.
Currently, the calculation of EBITDA pre is based on EBIT. The future EBITDA pre will be based on the newly defined IFRS 18 operating profit or loss, to which we will add depreciation and amortization, as well as adjustable items. Without going into the details at this stage, our simulations suggest that the deviation of past and future EBITDA pre is less than 2%. With the introduction of IFRS 18, some definitions of some adjustments will be changing. We've prepared a slide in the appendix of this deck which explains these changes.
We will share more insights as we get closer to the implementation of IFRS 18. With that, let us move on to the performance analysis of the three businesses. I'm starting with Life Science on page nine. Life Science sales grew organically by 8% in Q2. Once again, Process Solutions was the key driver. We already highlighted in Q1, the business is benefiting from strong underlying demand, supported by temporarily stronger purchasing activity in APAC and new customer projects.
We saw this already towards the end of Q1, the temporary uplift continued into early Q2. Anticipated, however, it started to normalize over the course of the quarter. Beyond that, we do not see any unusual effects. We have neither experienced significant delays in customer projects, nor do we see a dependency on specific product groups. Our performance remains broad-based. That said, the assumption which we shared with you in our May call, namely a normalization in the second half of 2026, does remain valid.
As expected, the Process Solutions order book normalized in Q2. Advanced Solutions and Discovery Solutions are on track. Advanced Solutions grew 4% organically, with the research spending environment gradually improving. Discovery Solutions grew 2% organically despite a muted market environment, including continued softness in China. EBITDA pre increased to EUR 700 million with the margin expanding by 50 basis points to 29%. At the same time, we continue to invest in R&D as a key driver of our future growth and differentiation.
Examples of such investments include the launch of Viresolve Pro- S solution, which is a virus filtration solution designed to be more sustainable and to improve throughput for complex and high concentration monoclonal antibodies. We also introduced our first bio-based high-performance liquid chromatography, HPLC solvents, which emit around 26% less CO2 equivalent on average without compromising on performance. Zooming out, there are two more topics. First, tariff refunds.
Effects from tariff refunds to customers were not material in Q2. For the full year, these effects are reflected in our updated guidance, which Kai will explain in detail in a few minutes. Second, of course, our plans to acquire Bio-Techne. No news is good news. We are on track. Regarding the account and treatment of the pending acquisition of Bio-Techne, let me remind you that we will see material effects such as recognition of transaction costs only after closing, which is expected by the end of this year or in early 2027.
Following closing, we would expect immediate EBITDA pre-merger accretion. We estimate the run rate cost synergies to amount to approximately EUR 140 million by year three after closing, the year in which we also expect to see EPS pre accretion on group level. Over to healthcare, which is on page 10. Reported healthcare sales increased by 2.4% to EUR 2.2 billion. Organically, sales declined by 3.4%, that was more than offset by positive portfolio effects from our rare disease portfolio at 5.4%.
In rare diseases, Auxilium and GOMEKLI delivered a combined sales of EUR 207 million in H1, which is fully in line with our guidance. We also saw initial sales of Pimicotinib following the private market launch in China. Cardiometabolic sales increased 1% organically amid ongoing constraints in the Middle East and partial reversal of the positive phasing in China, which we flagged to you in Q1.
Fertility and endocrinology sales were about stable. Gonal-f pricing in the U.S. started normalizing, while Pergoveris continued to deliver double-digit growth and Saizen was slightly up against tough comps. Specialty care declined 6% organically, mainly reflecting Mavenclad's loss of market exclusivity in the U.S. and the competitive environment for BAVENCIO. Notably, Erbitux sales increased 5% organically.
We also have seen progress in the late phases of our pipeline. We have dosed the first patient in our phase III study of Precem-TcT, which is our first-in-class anti-CEACAM5 ADC in third line metastatic colorectal cancer. Also, FDA has granted breakthrough therapy designation to enpatoran for the treatment of lupus with active cutaneous manifestations. We also recently received file acceptance from the FDA for Pergoveris. However, uncertainty remains. Healthcare EBITDA pre was EUR 747 million with a still strong margin of 34.7%.
This is supported by a favorable product mix and disciplined cost management, partially offsetting higher R&D investments reflecting the ramp-up of our phase III pipeline project, as well as launch investments in rare diseases. Let's move to Electronics. Electronics delivered a strong quarter with organic sales growth accelerating to 11.7%. Reported sales were EUR 871 million, reflecting the portfolio effect from the divestment of Surface Solutions.
Semi Solutions grew 17% organically, fueled by continued demand in semi materials, driven by advanced nodes in both logic and memory. Overall, growth was supported by all parts of the portfolio. Delivery Systems & Services also had a better quarter due to the finalization of a large project and against a low base. Therefore, I would caution against extrapolating this trend. Optronics remained around stable. However, the business continues to face headwinds from softer demand for consumer electronics influenced by high memory prices.
This could result in a year-over-year decline in net sales in the second half. EBITDA pre increased to EUR 244 million with the margin expanding to 28%. This represents a sequential increase versus the underlying EBITDA pre-margin in Q1 of around 200 basis points. As a reminder, the EBITDA pre-margin in Q2 2025 of 15.1% was suppressed by one-offs. Adjusted for these effects, the year-over-year underlying margin increase would have still been insignificant. Turning briefly to key developments in our balance sheet.
Total assets stood at EUR 52.7 billion at the end of June. Cash and cash equivalents decreased mainly due to repayment of euro-denominated bonds. Receivables increased due to continued strong sales performance while inventories increased mainly in Life Science and Healthcare to support future growth. Worth noting is that we saw the main uplift of receivables and inventories in Q1. The incremental increase was basically driven by FX effects in Q2. Intangible assets increased mainly due to foreign exchange effects.
On the liability side, financial debt increased compared with year-end 2025 as a repayment of euro-denominated bonds was offset by an increase of financial liabilities to related parties and by the U.S. dollar bond increase to foreign exchange effects. The equity ratio increased slightly to 57%. I would like to round off with a few remarks on cash flow. Operating cash flow in Q2 was EUR 605 million, up from EUR 567 million in the prior year quarter, despite a decrease in profit after tax.
Profit after tax was lower due to reorganization provisions, higher R&D expenses, as well as increased depreciations and amortizations, mainly due to the acquisition of SpringWorks. Most categories in the cash flow statement showed favorable underlying improvements, and I want to highlight net working capital optimization in particular. These effects were offset by temporary changes in the tax balance and paid bond interests.
The underlying cash generation has visibly improved in recent months and will remain a strong focus going forward as we strive for fast deleveraging after closing of the planned Bio-Techne acquisition. Investing cash flow was higher, driven by short-term investments and payments for the acquisition of the JSR chromatography business. Financing cash flow reflected the repayment of the euro-denominated bonds. With that, back to Kai.

Kai Beckmann (Chairman of the Executive Board and Group CEO, Merck): Thanks a lot, Helene, let me now round it off with guiding you through our raised guidance for 2026 on slides 15 and 16. We now expect organic growth in group net sales of 1%-3%, compared with 0%-3% previously. Compared to the previous guidance, we see easing headwinds from foreign exchange rates. Foreign exchange impact is now expected to amount to -2% to 0% after -3% to -1% previously. Hence, group net sales are expected to reach around EUR 21 billion-EUR 21.8 billion.
The midpoint of this range equals the high end of our previous net sales guidance of EUR 20.4 billion-EUR 21.4 billion. For EBITDA pre, we now expect EUR 5.9 billion-EUR 6.3 billion compared with EUR 5.7 billion-EUR 6.1 billion previously. This reflects an organic development of 0%-3%, compared with -2% to +2% before. EPS pre is expected to be in the range of EUR 7.90-EUR 8.60, a 5% increase compared to the previous range of EUR 7.50-EUR 8.20. At the business sector level, you can see how the numbers come together.
For Life Science, we are raising the lower end of our expected organic net sales growth range from 4% to 5%. The new range of 5%-7% organic sales growth also includes a potential headwind from tariff refunds to customers of around EUR 40 million. EBITDA pre organic growth in Life Science is now expected in a range of 5%-8%, compared with 4%-8% previously. The range of around EUR 2.6 billion-EUR 2.8 billion remains unchanged.
For Healthcare, we now expect organic net sales development of -4% to -2%, compared with -6% to -3% in May. This is driven by our assumptions on Mavenclad U.S. now assuming zero sales as of August and slightly better performance in the other parts of the business. Our assumptions continue to exclude a potential Pergoveris launch in the U.S. in 2026. As of July 1st, Auxilium and GOMEKLI will be recognized as organic sales.
The related portfolio effect is therefore limited to the first half of the year and amounts to +2.4% or EUR 207 million in absolute terms. EBITDA pre in Healthcare is expected to be around EUR 2.8 billion-EUR 3 billion compared with EUR 2.6 billion-EUR 2.8 billion previously. For Electronics, we are raising our organic net sales growth guidance to 6%-9% from 3%-7% previously, the portfolio effect from Surface Solutions divestment amounts to minus EUR 245 million.
EBITDA pre for Electronics is now expected to be around EUR 1 billion, compared with the previous range of around EUR 0.9 billion-EUR 1 billion. The respective range for organic growth moves from 21%-27% to 25%-29%, reflecting the recovery and operating leverage in Semi Solutions. With that, allow me to conclude with a brief summary before we open the lines for Q&A. We delivered a robust second quarter with accelerating organic sales growth and even stronger organic EBITDA pre growth.
The first half of the year confirms the resilience of our broad portfolio and the relevance of the strategic priorities we outlined earlier this year. We are encouraged by the continued momentum in Life Science and Electronics, we remain disciplined in Healthcare as we invest in our launches and pipeline.
Our increased full year guidance reflects these positive developments, we will remain focused on executing our strategic agenda, including a potential start of the integration of Bio-Techne following a successful closing, potentially at the end of this year or early next year. Cost discipline will remain a priority, while at the same time we continue to invest in innovation to sustain profitable growth in the future. With that, I will now hand it back to Heidi to open the lines for questions.

Operator: Thank you. We will now begin our question and answer session. If you have a question for our speakers, please dial star one one on your telephone keypad now to enter the queue. Once your name has been announced, you can ask a question. If you are using speaker equipment today, please lift the handset before making your selection. One moment, please, for our first question. Your first question comes from the line of Peter Verdult from BNP Paribas. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Peter Verdult (Managing Director and Pharmaceuticals Equity Research, BNP Paribas): Thank you. Peter Verdult, BNP Paribas. Two questions to kick off for Kai or Helene. The stock's done well this year, the key debate in the market is quickly turning to 2027 and the ability for Merck to post organic growth, given the Mavenclad and Life Science customer stocking tailwinds you've enjoyed this year. I realize you're not going to give guidance per se on a Q2 conference call, would like to kick the tires with you, engage your current level of confidence about organic growth prospects in 2027.
Secondly, in the more sort of gnarly for Danny, good to hear that Pergoveris has been filed. Potential uncertainties were flagged in the preparatory remarks. Can you confirm these comments relate to the label you get rather than the approvability of Pergoveris? If that is correct, can you just remind us what the best case scenario would look like with respect to the FDA label, should the product get approved? Thank you.

Kai Beckmann (Chairman of the Executive Board and Group CEO, Merck): Peter, thanks for the 2027 question. We upgraded our guidance twice this year. Life Science, Electronics showing really robust growth, and Healthcare is holding up reasonably well amid the generic competition we're seeing. As we look at the 2027 fundamentals and the underlying trends are very well intact for Life Science and Electronics, and Healthcare is focused on executing the strategic agenda in next year. Basically 2027 should be well in line with our projections from last year's CMD.
Just as a first highlight, we'll be very much in line with our projections from last year's CMD. Obviously, of course, the comps will be tough for Mavenclad, no doubt. Process Solutions will have a high comparison base in the first half of 2027 as we compare it with a very strong first half in 2026. Looking at the proposed transaction to acquire Bio-Techne. If closed in line with our plans, it would add close to 5% to group sales growth and about 10% to Life Science alone.
Also, the transaction would be immediately accretive to group EBITDA pre margin, and we are committed to EPS pre accretion in year three post-closing. That should give you some color on how we look into 2027 from today's perspective. As you rightly said, of course, we're not providing any 2027 guidance at this time of the year, but just some color on the question you were asking. I hand it to Danny for the second question.

Danny Bar-Zohar (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Healthcare, Merck): Yes. Thanks, Kai. Hi, Peter. Yes, the FDA has notified us late last week of the acceptance of the full BLA submission. This is per se, this is good news. It's a good milestone. Pergoveris is a great product. As Helene said, however, the uncertainty remains over the potential approval. I will give you a little bit more color on that. First of all, just to frame it, Pergoveris is the only recombinant FSH LH combination in the market. I would say an important innovation for patients who need that.
The product is approved in 116 countries around the globe, including China since February this year. It's been growing and taking share in every market we're available, underpinning the value that it brings to women struggling to have a baby. Matter of fact, over 6 million babies have been born worldwide with our fertility medicines. In 2026 only, year to date, Pergoveris generated sales of over EUR 300 million, five years CAGR of over 20%.
Of course, we are keen to bring Pergoveris also to the U.S., one of the largest and most innovative pharma markets. We were, I would say, delighted to have received the CNPV as part of our agreement with the White House at the end of last year. As we told you before, the procedure as itself is quite new, and the submission is based on a lot of legacy data, mostly generated outside of the U.S.
You also need to keep in mind that in the past years, we have already had intense discussions with the FDA regulator and could not agree on a path forward. We feel there is considerable uncertainty, to Helene's point, about whether the package now is sufficient for the FDA to approve. You also asked how could a best case label look like. Here, I would easily refer you to the EU label or the Canadian label so you can get a sense. That is where we are right now with Pergoveris.

Peter Verdult (Managing Director and Pharmaceuticals Equity Research, BNP Paribas): Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. We will take our next question. Your next question comes from Matthew Weston from UBS. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Matthew Weston (Managing Director and Pharmaceuticals Equity Research, UBS): Thank you. Two questions, please. The first on Process Solutions and this comment on normalizing over the quarter. I think I understand, but I'm going to ask you to spell it out. Are we saying that the extra demand has stopped, but the extra inventory remains with the customer, and therefore at some point in time going forward, we should expect that inventory to unwind? I guess previously you've said no customer is greater than 5% of PS sales, but I assume we can't say something similar for the inventory.
It will be more concentrated. Secondly, on atacicept royalties, there's been a lot of debate about their leverage to Merck in the market. I know you've said it before. Can you please remind us how much of the royalty you receive and how much you have to pass on?

Jean-Charles Wirth (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Life Science, Merck): Hello, Matthew. Jean-Charles speaking. Hope you are doing fine. Let me try to clarify the situation. I will start with the Q2. In Q2, in Process Solutions, we grew organically 15%, and I would like to give you some background behind. We have five key driver. The first one, the market demand remains healthy. The second driver, we continue to benefit from our new go-to-market model, and few months ago, I mentioned that we're improving our service level, which have a positive impact on our overall performance.
The third element is linked to what I said back in May when I mentioned that we have observed, especially in March, special buyer pattern from very few Asian customer linked to our ongoing geopolitical, call it Middle East conflict. The fourth driver was exceptional growth in China, mainly due to the fact that some customer order equipment in order to build new plant. The last element is related to the fact that we enjoy some boosts on order intake and sales from non-repeat order, which are related to our integrated workflow solution offering.
To answer your question, from the five driver, the last three are the one who are boosting our performance in Q2. To your question concerning the inventory destocking, we do not anticipate any destocking effect in 2026. You should assume in your model that if we have some inventory destocking effect, it may take place in 2027. The fourth driver was exceptional growth in China, mainly due to the fact that some customer order equipment in order to build new plant.
And the last element is related to the fact that we enjoy some boosts on order intake and sales from non-repeat order, which are related to our integrated workflow solution offering. To answer your question, from the five driver, the last three are the one who are boosting our performance in Q2. To your question concerning the inventory destocking, we do not anticipate any destocking effect in 2026. But you should assume in your model that if we have some inventory destocking effect, it may take place in 2027.

Danny Bar-Zohar (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Healthcare, Merck): Regarding atacicept, yes, the drug received approval for IgA nephropathy several weeks ago. To your question, Matthew, it's fair to assume that there remains a meaningful obligation from Merck to BMS when it comes to potential milestones and royalties. As we are expecting a launch here, in virtually every scenario, the net royalty rate upside would remain for us in the single-digit % range.

Matthew Weston (Managing Director and Pharmaceuticals Equity Research, UBS): Thank you. Can I just push you? I know there are about EUR 600 million of milestones in the original out licensing agreement. Is it fair to assume that there will be milestones also to Merck over the course of the launch and commercial revenue hits?

Danny Bar-Zohar (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Healthcare, Merck): The answer is yes.

Matthew Weston (Managing Director and Pharmaceuticals Equity Research, UBS): Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. We will take our next question. Your question comes from Sachin Jain from Bank of America. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Sachin Jain (VP, Bank of America): Hi there. Just a few questions, please. Just a follow on the Process Solutions. Could you confirm that Process Solutions for the full year is still in the upper end of the 8%-12% you referenced on the last call? Or does the 1H strength take you slightly above that, just given what would be implied for the second half?
Second question on Semiconductor Solutions is around the sustainability of the mid-teens materials and what is assumed within the guide. I wonder if I could just clarify the 2027 comment, Kai, and apologies. It sounded to me like that Bio-Techne was the main offset for the tougher comps in the base. Or are you confirming mid-single-digit organic growth, which is what you said at the 2025 CMD? Apologies for that clarification.

Kai Beckmann (Chairman of the Executive Board and Group CEO, Merck): I'll take the 2027 question first, Sachin, just to clarify. The comment on the commitment from the CMD is organic, of course, and the second comment on Bio-Techne then is, of course, the reported effect. Just these two elements I want to highlight, but important is the comment from CMD is the organic part.

Jean-Charles Wirth (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Life Science, Merck): Sachin, Jean-Charles speaking. Let me answer the first question concerning Process Solutions. First of all, I would like to take the opportunity to talk about our book-to-bill ratio. If you look our book-to-bill ratio year to date June, so I'm talking about 1H, our book-to-bill ratio is above 1. What we assume now, we expect a normalization of our Process Solutions growth during the second half, but our book-to-bill ratio should remain above one. In this context, we see a strong underlying of our growth.
If you think about the range we gave, 8%-12%, we are thinking to land in the upper range of the guidance for the full year.

Benjamin Hein (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Electronics, Merck): Hey, Sachin, this is Ben speaking. Thank you very much for your question on Semi. Just to recap, Semiconductor Solutions grew 17% in Q2, this business is the growth driver for the broader Electronics business, both in this year as well as in the midterm. Just as a reminder, Semiconductor Solutions consists of semiconductor materials, which is around 65% of overall Electronics sales, as well as the Delivery Systems & Services business, in short, DS&S, which accounts for less than 15% of the total Electronics sales.
Regarding semiconductor materials, coming to your question, sales were up in the low double-digit percentage point organically. Why? Because it's driven pretty much by the AI-related applications in advanced nodes, both on logic as well as memory. It's also good to see that all parts of the portfolio contribute to this growth. As you remember, over the past 10 quarters, we have seen an average of low teens growth, in this business. In addition, in Q2, we also saw DS&S contributing to Semiconductor Solutions growth.
That's unlikely to repeat. Our expectations for DS&S only moderately improve. We see a broad stable outlook for the remaining quarters in this year. Just to take a step back, by and large, especially the leading-edge customers that contribute to the AI-driven growth remain capacity constrained both this year into the second half as well as well into 2027.

Jean-Charles Wirth (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Life Science, Merck): Hey, Sachin, Jean-Charles speaking. Just to avoid any misunderstanding, when I mentioned the 8% to 12% organic growth for the full year, I was talking of the Process Solutions portfolio. Just to give you some flavor, I confirm that we still have now ongoing interaction with customer. We are tracking our book-to-bill ratio, order intake, order book. What I try to tell you is we feel very confident for 2026 on Process Solutions.

Operator: Thank you. We will take our next question. Your question comes from the line of James Quigley from Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

James Quigley (Executive Director, Goldman Sachs): Great. Thank you for taking my question. I've got two, please, and I think both for JC. First one, no surprise, following up on the PS stocking. You gave a fairly big if when you're thinking about the destocking potential impact in 2027. How much visibility do you have there over the customer's inventory? Is there a scenario where the higher inventory levels could actually be the new normal for those customers or could reverse or destock on a pretty slow cadence so that the headwind in 2027 is actually pretty minimal?
Then second of all, we've heard a lot in the last 18 months or so about the CapEx investments by your pharma customers in the U.S. Have you started to see any progress with respect to the planned significant capacity expansions? Presumably as a consumables-focused portfolio, it will take a bit of time before it will flow through to Merck.
Have you started any discussions or pitches or RFPs or anything like that with customers as they start to assess their CapEx plan? How are you ensuring that Merck will get its fair share of that capacity as it comes online? Thank you.

Jean-Charles Wirth (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Life Science, Merck): To your first question about the PS stocking, I will say as of now, keep in mind that we're in July. We have limited visibility for 2027. That said, what I can tell you is from a quality of our order, we are back to pre-COVID level in term of order lead time. We feel very comfortable with, call it maybe inventory impact only in 2027, not in 2026. To your second question concerning CapEx by large pharma customer, the answer is yes, we have ongoing discussion with the large pharma customer.
I visited one few weeks ago, and I have one important meeting which is scheduled in September with one of our largest customer. I take the opportunity to mention back to the question of Matthew, that our largest customer is less than 1%-2% of our total revenue in any business unit, call it Process Solutions, Advanced Solutions, or Discovery Solutions. On CapEx, yes, we have exchanged, yes, we have meetings, but it's too early to say to move forward with a clear view.
We have ongoing discussion. Maybe my last comment, keep in mind that most of our portfolio is consumable driven, not equipment. I expect that we'll see some benefit at some stage, but short term, no.

James Quigley (Executive Director, Goldman Sachs): Great. Thank you.

Jean-Charles Wirth (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Life Science, Merck): Thank you.

Operator: Thank you. We will take our next question. Your next question comes from Richard Vosser from JP Morgan. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Richard Vosser (Analyst, JPMorgan): Hi. Thanks for taking my question. A couple, please. First of all, on the CEACAM5 ADC, there was some interesting data at ASCO in another tumor, pancreatic. Just thinking about the potential development in further indications, further tumors beyond third-line colorectal cancer, are you still looking for a partner to further increase investment in the product? How are you thinking about this going forward?
Second question, sorry to belabor the point on Process Solutions. Just second half, it seems that you're pointing towards an underlying growth rate, something like 10%-12%, but we should deduct tariff returns of about EUR 40 million from that. Are there any other headwinds that we should think about in the second half? And then just one final little bit on Process Solutions.
The new market model you referenced, should we think about this actually allowing you to be more competitive, maybe, dare I say, gain some market share against some of your competitors here? Is this something we should see or a little bit early for this? Thanks very much.

Danny Bar-Zohar (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Healthcare, Merck): Okay. Hi, Richard. It's Danny. I'll take the first question on the Precem-TcT, the CEACAM5. Yes, we are very proud of this first-in-class ADC, with data presented at ASCO first in colorectal cancer that keeps on very encouraging. You are right. At the CMD last year, we told you that we would be looking into the opportunity to partner this ADC, and indeed, we have had very good discussions with several interested parties over the past couple of months, I would say.
What we also said at the CMD, I said that personally, including David, is that we will be super disciplined in allocating capital and concentrating around a single asset with a lot of correlated risk. All in all, we concluded that we will not pursue partnering of Precem-TcT at that point. We will continue developing the compound in third-line metastatic colorectal cancer.
This is a huge global phase III study. It's a meaningful opportunity for us, and we can do so on our own without compromising on our strategic imperative, as I said, to reduce high capital intensity on correlated risk. When it comes to earlier lines of treatment, as well as the data that you mentioned for pancreatic cancer, first of all, we are committed to extract the value of this compound, but we will do it in a stage-gated, and I would say, very disciplined manner.
We will need to see how the colorectal cancer study progresses, and then we will take additional decisions on combinations and other tumors. The data in pancreatic cancer is indeed positive. It says that the drug is active, still cautious, and we will update as data comes.

Jean-Charles Wirth (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Life Science, Merck): Hey, Richard, Jean-Charles speaking. On your first question concerning Process Solutions for H2. If you look H1, we are currently off to a very, very good start. I said that for Process Solutions for the full year, we expect to be within the range of 8%-12%. If you peel the onion and you go one level deeper, in the high range of this guidance. If you do the math, you know exactly what should be our organic growth for H2. As of now, we don't see any headwinds on speed. Headwinds, again, I would like to talk about normalization for H2.
Concerning the process market model, the go-to market, overall, we are making good progress. We are completely done with the redesign. Everything is set, sales incentive, territory mapping, and the feedback of our customer is extremely positive. I'm very pleased with where we stand today. Too early to say that we are more competitive or we are gaining market share, but you should assume that I have a big smile and I'm very, very happy where we stand.

Operator: Thank you. We will take our next question. Your next question comes from Charles Pitman-King from Barclays. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Charles Pitman-King (VP of European Pharmaceuticals Equity Research, Barclays): Hi. Thanks so much for taking my questions. Two from me, please. Firstly, for Danny, just thinking about Mavenclad and the U.S. strategy and outlook. Based on the IQVIA data, it looks like broadly U.S. prescription volumes of cladribine have actually been declining despite typical generic competition driving volumes up. Just wondering if you can confirm that this is because of an intentional reduction in the marketing efforts of Merck, an increased share loss to competition, or illustrative of just a poor capture rate from IQVIA.
If you could just give us a few more details around how you're currently defending on price or volume and how you expect erosion to take place from August 2027, when the European patent goes. Just the second question, please, on electronic margins and DS&S. Just obviously noting that DS&S has been a bit lumpy, I'm wondering if you could give us a bit more insight into how close we are to reaching a more normalized growth rate, noting you're saying it's going to moderate in the second half of this year.
Just trying to think also what the impact has been on margins in 2Q from the DS&S project and how we should think about margins into 2H, given 1H came in around 31% versus the full year implied 29%-30%, implying that's greatly de-risked. Thanks very much.

Danny Bar-Zohar (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Healthcare, Merck): Hi, Charles. It's Danny. I'll start with the question on Mavenclad. Yeah, when it comes to Mavenclad in the U.S., Q2 sales were, I would say almost on par with Q1, albeit the trend started weakening towards the end of the quarter, just as an FYI. Indeed, Mavenclad is showing slower generic erosion versus prior analogs, given the slower generic registration and limited penetration. We have two generics approved.
However, more generics are lined up for approval in due course, two of them potentially entering the market, according to our assumptions still in this quarter, in the third quarter. As such, if we're talking about our ability to guide, we will stay with this guidance methodology. Just as an FYI, when it comes to Mavenclad outside of the U.S., the growth has been very strong. Europe, for example, up 32% in Q2.
Very strong commercial execution, significant uptake of year one patients. If we are talking about the full year 2026 outside of the U.S., we expect a double-digit growth for Mavenclad. As you said, the loss of or the expiration of the regulatory exclusivity in Europe is expected in August 2027. We do have SPCs. However, I would strongly recommend that for modeling purposes, you would take the August 2027.

Benjamin Hein (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Electronics, Merck): Hi, Charles, it's Ben. Thank you very much for your questions. Let me start with DS&S. When you look at Q2, we actually saw DS&S contributing to Semiconductor Solutions growth, specifically due to a finalization of a large project in that quarter. As you know, it comes after a period of relatively weak performance, after which the growth for DS&S has normalized towards the end of last year, and as we reported last time, was flat quarter-over-quarter in Q1. Our expectation for DS&S only moderately improves.
We see broadly stable outlook in the second half of this year compared to the second half of last year. Just as a reminder, DS&S has three components. One is the large projects business, which we manage opportunistically, so don't put it in your base. The second one is equipment for gas delivery, but also chemical delivery. The third element is the recurring service model. On the margin question itself, we've done a good job in Q2 on managing our margin. We have committed to you that we will work on margin expansion quarter-over-quarter, year-over-year.
We've delivered on that commitment. We saw around 200 basis points increase quarter-over-quarter from Q1, so it's a solid expansion. When you look at it, we stand at 28% EBITDA pre-margin in Q2, which is up significantly from the 15.1 in Q2 last year. I have to say it's a clean quarter, so don't account for any significant one-time effects in Q2 this year. However, as you remember, Q2 last year was suppressed due to mainly two one-time effects that we highlighted.
On the reported EBITDA pre-margin, it's mildly supported, as Helene said, by FX tailwinds of roughly 1%, as well as the portfolio effect, which we've seen of around minus 6% from the divestment of Surface Solutions. Overall, the EBITDA pre was up 87.5% organically year-over-year. We see expanding margins. We continue to work on structural margin progression, and what's behind that is, of course, the portfolio effect from Surface Solutions with roughly 100 basis points annualized benefit.
Second, from increased volumes, we see operational leverage. Third, we actively manage our cost position, as highlighted earlier. Last, but definitely not the least, we also see a positive mix effect due to the strong demand driven by AI applications in the market, especially data center build-outs.

Charles Pitman-King (VP of European Pharmaceuticals Equity Research, Barclays): Thank you so much.

Operator: Thank you. We will take our next question. Your next question comes from Falko Friedrichs from Deutsche Bank. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Falko Friedrichs (Director of Equity Research, Deutsche Bank): Thank you. Two questions, please. The first one is on the Discovery Solutions business within Life Science. Could you provide a bit more color on the end market trends outside of China and especially in the U.S. that you've witnessed in the second quarter? My second question is on the semi materials business again. Is there a positive inflection of this AI-related demand for your products that you're starting to notice? Thank you.

Jean-Charles Wirth (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Life Science, Merck): Hello, Falko. Jean-Charles speaking. Let me start with your question on Life Science related to Discovery Solutions. First of all, I would like to mention that we are growing now for four consecutive quarter. Back to the comment I made on the go-to-market. We are now fully leveraging our multi-channel approach. What I mean by multi-channel approach, we are selling directly, we are using our e-commerce platform. We are also selling via dealers, and we see the benefit to have a better focus on this portfolio.
Concerning the customer segments, all segments are improving, except academia, which remain quite soft, mainly in two countries, U.S.A. and China. That said, talking about China, I also mentioned a few weeks ago that we have just promoted a new head of China. This person reports to me, he's part of the executive team. We are currently in the process to assessing what could we do in China strategically in order to make sure that we are going to win in this market.

Benjamin Hein (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Electronics, Merck): Hey, Falko, it's Ben. Let me take the AI-related question. As we said earlier, we already participate today from AI-driven growth. When you look at the end market, overall data center build-outs continue to be strong. At the same time, consumer electronics remain a bit muted. We are seeing the growth mainly coming from the AI-driven segment. Here, when you break it down, it's both memory as well as advanced logic processing. That's not a new phenomenon, but definitely it's an ongoing driver.
We've also updated our guidance, as Kai said earlier today, to 6%-9% sales growth for the year to account for that demand growth. Again, I want to remind us to mind the capacity constraints of our customers, especially in the AI segment, which are already happening today and which we believe will extend well into the next year as well as we debottleneck as an industry.

Falko Friedrichs (Director of Equity Research, Deutsche Bank): Okay, thank you.

Operator: Thank you. We will take our next question. The question comes from the line of Rajesh Kumar from HSBC. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Rajesh Kumar (Managing Director and Head of US & EU Healthcare Equity Research, HSBC): Hi, good afternoon. Thanks for taking my question. Just on the Process Solutions first half growth, the effects you have talked about, can you help us understand how that might have impacted or hampered your operating margins for the Life Sciences division? I.e., was the incremental cost of delivery significantly higher than normal or lower and the incremental drop-through margin, so that when we are modeling our first half for 2027, we are anchoring it off the right kind of run rate assumptions on drop-through margin?
That's the first question. Second question, just on the book-to-bill side. I know you have historically tracked the duration of order books. It might be a bit more subjective than objective in terms of numbers. When you think of your book-to-bill, are you seeing any meaningful duration changes in the order book, i.e., are the order lead times getting much longer or shorter compared to the prior quarter or long-term averages? Any color there would be much appreciated. Thank you.

Jean-Charles Wirth (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Life Science, Merck): Hey, Kumar. Let me try to answer. The line was bad, I'm not sure I catch your first question well, but to my understanding, it's about our profit margin evolution. As you can imagine, we are marching towards quality growth P&L where we want the bottom line to grow faster than the top line. However, you need to keep in mind that we still face some absorption or extra absorption linked to the startup costs related to our region, four region initiatives where we just open or we are in the process to open new manufacturing sites.
Just to name a few, last year we opened Blarney in Cork for Process Solutions, and you should assume that now we are in the ramp-up phase, which means that we have more costs than last year. In the near future, actually in October, we are going to open a new manufacturing site in Asia, in South Korea, Daejeon, again for bioprocessing. We are currently in the ramp-up phase as we speak. What I mean, we are adding headcounts without yet doing production. It's extra cost for us.
On top, based on the current performance of Life Science and Process Solutions, we are also increasing on purpose R&D investments. Earlier in the call, Helene mentioned two new products launch, Viresolve and HPLC Green Solvent for discovery. I could add the CLX eight for Lab Water and end. What we try to do, based on the current performance, we want to accelerate our innovation engine to make sure that we improve the way we supply our customer, the way we offer full solution in their workflow and so forth.
This is on your first question. Concerning the book-to-bill structure. In the past, I mentioned that we rebuilt our book-to-bill structure back to 2019, pre-COVID. We call it the Rainbow Report. What I can tell you is roughly 75%-80% of our order have a lead time of one to six months, this is exactly where we stand at the end of June 2026.

Rajesh Kumar (Managing Director and Head of US & EU Healthcare Equity Research, HSBC): Very helpful. Thank you very much.

Operator: We will take our next question. Your next question comes from the line of Simon Baker from Rothschild & Co Redburn. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Simon Baker (Partner and the Head of Global Biopharma Research, Rothschild and Co Redburn): Thank you for taking my questions. Two, if I may, please. Firstly, a broader question on M&A and business development post the Bio-Techne deal. I just wonder if you could remind us about your capacity, focus, and appetite for transactions following the Bio-Techne deal, then moving to Semiconductor Solutions. Kai, you mentioned metrology in your opening comments and another company specifically called out growth from AI-related metrology. I just wanted to see if you were seeing any effects from that.
More broadly, I wonder if you could update us on the outlook for memory capacity. We've seen some early signs that maybe capacity from a very constrained position is beginning to expand. You've probably got better oversight than anyone else, really, across that. Any update there would be very helpful. Thank you.

Kai Beckmann (Chairman of the Executive Board and Group CEO, Merck): Simon, let me take the M&A question. Of course, we are diligently working on Bio-Techne right now. That requires all focus on our side, preparation in line with what we can already prepare, what we are allowed to prepare, and working on the execution of that deal. That's our top-notch focus. Then, of course, I shared in the strategy update our very strong intent to replenish our early phase pipeline in Healthcare and as an important strategy.
Of course, overall, we are and we continue to be committed in strengthening our growth drivers, Electronics and Life Science overall. That is what we work on. We shared with you in the financing of the current deal. I think you can do the math on what could go beyond that. Of course, most importantly, we have to be able to execute on these deals diligently. Integration is key. That gives you a frame of what we want to do, what we need to do, of course, limited by what we are able to do at the end of the day.
It's a pretty clear and straightforward plan on our priorities. I will hand over for metrology inspection to Ben, as he will focus on this one.

Benjamin Hein (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Electronics, Merck): Yeah. Thank you very much, Kai. Thanks, Simon, for the question. Let me recap on metrology and inspection. We acquired that capability and metrology tools measure critical parameters in chip manufacturing, such as depth, step heights, and thickness, and they really enable real-time adjustments that improve process control. That becomes really important, especially in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, where quality and purity requirements get tighter and tighter, especially as we move towards advanced packaging.
Inspection tools, on the other hand, detect a wide array of defect types, ensuring the highest quality standards as well. Together, these technologies really enhance manufacturing yields, reduce production costs, and accelerate time to market for the next generation of semiconductor innovation with our customers. It's a relatively small business for us. The integration is going extremely well.
As Kai and Helene mentioned earlier today, we just opened a new facility to be able to support our customers from a capacity, but also from a capability point of view. Regarding memory, the reality today is there is a shortage of memory chips. Prices for advanced memory chips are very high. We expect this trend or this situation to continue at least until the second half of 2027. We work very hard day and night with our customers on debottlenecking this capacity, it's not going to go away tomorrow.

Simon Baker (Partner and the Head of Global Biopharma Research, Rothschild and Co Redburn): Great. Thanks so much.

Operator: Thank you. We will take our next question. The question comes from Peter Spengler from DZ Bank. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Peter Spengler (Analyst, DZ Bank): Hello. Thank you for taking my two questions. First, on Electronics, you reported 17% organic growth in Semiconductor Solutions, but only 12% for Electronics division overall. What explains the 5% gap? The second question is on the bioprocessing market dynamics. A major American competitor reported low single-digit growth in bioprocessing for Q2 due to different reasons. Are you benefiting from this softer competitor performance, or are you facing the same customer shipment delays? Thank you.

Benjamin Hein (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Electronics, Merck): Thank you very much. Let me start with the Electronics question. When we recap the different businesses, Semiconductor Solutions grew 17%. Overall, as you rightly state, we are around 12% sales growth in Electronics in Q2. What explains the difference is that Optronics is largely flat in this quarter.

Jean-Charles Wirth (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Life Science, Merck): Concerning your question about the bioprocess markets, linked to the go-to-market reorganization, we moved back the customer in the center of what we do. We have increased the number of interaction we have with customer. While I will not comment on the competition, what I can tell you is concerning Merck Life Science and bioprocessing per se, it's business as usual. We don't see any variance or any trend which are abnormal.

Florian Schröder (Head of Investor Relations, Merck): Heidi, we would have time for one last question, please.

Operator: Thank you. Please stand by. Your final question comes from the line of Oliver Metzger from Oddo BHF. Please go ahead. Your line is open.

Oliver Metzger (Analyst, Oddo BHF): Okay. Good afternoon. Thanks for taking my questions. First one is for J.C., on Process Solutions. Just, you reflect the strong buying pattern, APAC. You mentioned also some stocking effects from Middle East conflict, but is there also some, say, improving fundamental demand? A second question for Ben on DS&S. In H2 last year, you reported some shifts of projects.
Would you describe the earlier than expected return to growth in Q2 as the result that some of these projects have come back, or do you still see them as part of your pipeline and just their timing is unknown? The last one quickly for Danny on fertility. It was stable development, and we saw, due to Gonal-f, some volatility over last quarters. Can you share more insights? What's currently holding the business back? Thank you.

Jean-Charles Wirth (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Life Science, Merck): Yeah, let me start with Process Solutions, J.C. speaking. We still believe the market for bioprocess remains very attractive, growing nine to 10%, and we believe that we are performing extremely well now for two quarters. Let me repeat what I said in term of key trends. Strong, healthy demand in the market. Nice benefit from our go-to-market model, where we improve our sales level and we move back and put back the customer in the center of what we do.
Then we observe, as I said, special buyer pattern from few Asian customer, exceptional growth in China, and finally, some one-time boost coming from order that we receive in order to improve the full workflow of our customers.

Benjamin Hein (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Electronics, Merck): Hi, Oliver, it's Ben. I'll cover the DS&S question. In Q2 2026, the main driver of the sales performance in DS&S is the finalization of one major large project that we already had in the pipeline, so that was already in execution. In H2 this year, we expect to be roughly flat compared to H2 last year.

Danny Bar-Zohar (Member of the Executive Board and CEO of Healthcare, Merck): Oliver, it's Danny. Regarding fertility, as you remember, with the new structure, we are lumping fertility and endocrinology and Saizen, I will try to give you the separate colors. With fertility and endocrinology, momentum improved, as Helene said, sequentially from -5% in Q1 to -1% in Q2. This was mainly driven by, I would say, the fading headwinds of the GONAL-f related to pricing in the U.S. As we told you before, we had a price reduction in Q2 last year, which started annualizing.
We also see slight rebalancing of the channel mix in light of MFN or the Trump Rx channel that we initiated. However, MFN also gives us a better visibility on the price going forward. This is one of the good things in this deal. Pergoveris, on the other hand, continued to grow double digits, 14% in Q2. This was slightly less than in prior quarters, mainly due to comps, nothing to worry about here, still double digit. In fact, we remain, I would say, super excited about the prospects for Pergoveris, including the recent China launch.
That's pretty much it. Together with it, there is Saizen, as we said, it was up in Q2, with very tough comps, that's the color on fertility.

Oliver Metzger (Analyst, Oddo BHF): Okay, great.

Florian Schröder (Head of Investor Relations, Merck): Thank you, Oliver. Thank you, everyone.

Oliver Metzger (Analyst, Oddo BHF): Thank you.

Florian Schröder (Head of Investor Relations, Merck): Thank you, Oliver. Thank you, everyone, who participated in today's discussion and for your continued interest in Merck. This concludes our Q2 2026 earnings call.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, thank you for your attendance. This call has been concluded. You may disconnect.

Operator: Dear ladies and gentlemen, welcome to the Merck Investor and Analyst Conference Call on second quarter 2026. As a reminder, all participants will be in a listen-only mode. I am now handing over to Florian Schröder, Head of Investor Relations, who will lead you through this conference. Please go ahead, sir.

Florian Schröder (Head of Investor Relations, Merck): Thank you very much, Heidi. Good afternoon, good morning, everyone, and welcome to our Q2 2026 results call. Thank you for joining us today. My name is Florian Schröder, and I'm the Head of Investor Relations at Merck. In our Q2 call today, Kai Beckmann, Group CEO, will begin with sharing an update on first steps since we announced our new strategic direction in May. Kai will provide a brief overview of our business performance and key developments in the second quarter as part of his executive summary.
Helene von Roeder, Group CFO, will guide you through the detailed financial overview. Before we move into the Q&A session, where we will be joined by Jean-Charles Wirth, CEO of Life Science, Danny Bar-Zohar, CEO of Healthcare, and Benjamin Hein, CEO of Electronics, Kai will share our updated outlook and guidance with you. With that, I'm pleased to hand it over to Kai to kick us off.

Kai Beckmann (Chairman of the Executive Board and Group CEO, Merck): Thank you, Florian, and good afternoon, good morning, and thanks to you all for joining us today. Before we get to the numbers, let me first give you a sense of where we stand strategically and highlight the milestones we have achieved in recent months since announcing our strategic direction in May. Each of these milestones addresses the evolving expectations of our customers and patients in an increasingly complex world.
Geopolitical tensions, shifting trade dynamics, active policy debates, and accelerating AI-driven technology rates are all shaping the environment in which we operate. In this context, only a clear plan and disciplined execution will move us closer to the sustainable, profitable growth we are building for our company. Allow me to share a few early proof points. Let me start with the signing of a definitive agreement to acquire Bio-Techne operation on June 25th.
Subject to regulatory approval and closing, Bio-Techne's complementary portfolio of high-quality reagents, analytical instruments, and diagnostic systems for precision medicine is expected to be immediately accretive to sales growth and margins. In parallel, we continue to invest in the capacity required to scale our manufacturing and R&D in Electronics, delivering precise, reliable, and scalable solutions across the semiconductor value chain. In June, we opened a new metrology and inspection site near Grenoble, France.
This EUR 20 million investment will expand our capacity for M&I tools in a key semiconductor hub. Our rare diseases portfolio continues to show strong momentum, and our pipeline has also advanced. Xevinapant and GOMEKLI both delivered quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year growth. In addition, Pimicotinib generated first sales in China and preparations for a U.S. launch are underway. The FDA granted breakthrough therapy designation for enpatoran for the treatment of lupus with active cutaneous manifestations.
The first patient was dosed in a phase III trial evaluating our anti-CEACAM5 antibody-drug conjugate, Precem-TcT for the third-line treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer. I stop here for today. Going forward, we will continue to share further proof points demonstrating that we are focusing investments where we see the strongest growth opportunities. We will make it easier for customers to work with us through more integrated solutions, we will share capabilities more effectively across the company.
We will continue to use partnerships and acquisitions where they accelerate progress. With that, let me turn to our operational and financial performance in the second quarter. Q2 was a pretty robust quarter. Following a solid start into the year, we continued to build growth momentum in the second quarter. Organic sales growth accelerated to 4.1%, supported by strong contributions from Life Science and Electronics.
In Life Science, growth was broad-based across all regions. Process Solutions again delivered strong growth, with sales up 15% organically. As a reminder, we expect the growth profile to normalize in the second half of the year. Advanced Solutions also contributed solid growth, while Discovery Solutions showed slight growth in a still muted market environment. In Healthcare, as I pointed out, rare diseases continued to make a meaningful contribution.
To better align with our operational structures, we have reorganized the remaining franchises. Cardiometabolic is now reported on a standalone basis, while Fertility & Endocrinology has been established as a newly created franchise. Both were broadly stable in the quarter. Specialty Care, which comprises of neurology and oncology assets, drove the overall organic decline in Healthcare, mainly reflecting the impact from Mavenclad in the U.S. and continued competition for Verzenio.
In Electronics, organic growth accelerated significantly to 12% in Q2. Semiconductor Solutions delivered very strong organic growth of 17%, fueled by continued momentum in advanced nodes. Optronics remained broadly stable, while headwinds in consumer electronics end markets are expected to increase further. As a result, we delivered on our ambition to generate profitable organic growth for the group while continuing to invest in innovation. EBITDA pre-margin expanded year-over-year by 1.6 percentage points to 29.4%.
Based on these robust results, we are raising our full year guidance, and I will share the details with you later in this call. Looking now at the group bridge in more detail on page six. Supported net sales increased by 3.4% year-over-year in Q2. Organic sales growth reached 4.1%, driven by Life Science and Electronics. A negative currency impact amounted to -1.1%, portfolio effects contributed 0.4%.
In Q1, organic growth of 2.9% was more than offset by disproportionate foreign exchange headwinds and negative portfolio effects. This quarter, the entire mix of organic growth, FX, and portfolio effects improved visibly, leading to an accelerated growth momentum. Organic EBITDA pre-growth was pleasing 9.3%, also driven by favorable comps in Electronics in Q2 2025. I'm handing over to Helene now to share further details.

Helene von Roeder (Member of the Executive Board and CFO, Merck): Thank you very much, Kai, a warm welcome also from my side. With that, let's dive into the overview of key financials on page eight. Net sales increased from EUR 5.255 billion in Q2 2025 to EUR 5.434 billion in Q2 2026. As mentioned already, this is driven by solid organic growth and easing currency headwinds, while portfolio effects in Healthcare and Electronics largely balanced each other out. EBITDA pre increased from EUR 1.46 billion to EUR 1.6 billion.
The organic increase by 9.3% was driven primarily by Life Science and Electronics, while foreign exchange and portfolio effects were close to neutral, leading to reported growth of 9.4%. EPS pre increased by 6.9% to EUR 2.16, this is achieved despite a visible increase in interest costs related to the financing of SpringWorks acquisition. However, for the full year, we slightly reduce our interest cost guidance, as you can see in the appendix. Operating cash flow increased moderately by 6.7% to EUR 605 million, which does not tell the full story.
Temporary effects are partially offsetting structural improvements, I will come back to this in a minute. Net financial debt increased to EUR 9.2 billion as of June 30th, mainly due to the dividend payment. The increase in working capital is largely a Q1 effect, with smaller increases in Q2, essentially relating to foreign exchange effects. One housekeeping item which I would like to flag already today is the potential impact of the implementation of IFRS 18. IFRS 18 will become effective as of January 2027.
Currently, the calculation of EBITDA pre is based on EBIT. The future EBITDA pre will be based on the newly defined IFRS 18 operating profit or loss, to which we will add depreciation and amortization, as well as adjustable items. Without going into the details at this stage, our simulations suggest that the deviation of past and future EBITDA pre is less than 2%. With the introduction of IFRS 18, some definitions of some adjustments will be changing. We've prepared a slide in the appendix of this deck which explains these changes.
We will share more insights as we get closer to the implementation of IFRS 18. With that, let us move on to the performance analysis of the three businesses.
